We next examined how injury severity affected pathogen resistance (Fig. 6d). Following infection with P. mirabilis, nymphs with injuries at levels 1–3 showed survival rates comparable with those of non-infected controls, whereas those at levels 4–6 exhibited significantly increased mortality (Fig. 6e). Similarly, following M. anisopliae infection, survival remained comparable with that of controls at injury levels 1–2 but declined significantly at levels 3–6 (Fig. 6f). These findings suggest that immune protection becomes insufficient as injury severity increases. To further assess the contribution of microbial guaiacol, we infected germ-depleted nymphs recolonized with wild-type or vdc-deficient E. hormaechei (Fig. 6g). At injury levels 1–3, nymphs harbouring wild-type bacteria exhibited significantly higher survival following pathogen challenge than those harbouring vdc mutants (Fig. 6h,i). However, at injury levels 4–6, mortality remained high regardless of bacterial genotype (Fig. 6h,i), indicating that guaiacol-mediated protection was insufficient under severe injury conditions.

It has been revealed that together, these results reveal an injury-severity-dependent trade-off between immune defence and cannibalistic risk. Following minor injury, microbial guaiacol enhances pathogen resistance without attracting conspecific predators, whereas severe injury results in increased guaiacol emission and cannibalistic attraction, while diminishing the protective benefits of guaiacol against infection.

Chemical signals, whether intrinsic or extrinsic, can be exploited by eavesdroppers to gain ecological advantages44. For example, stress-related corticosteroids and predator odours induce defensive responses in mice45,46, whereas insect pheromones can attract parasitoids or facilitate their avoidance47,48. Here we demonstrate that microbial volatile guaiacol links immune defence with cannibalistic behaviour in locusts. Production of guaiacol by the gut and haemolymph symbiont E. hormaechei increases rapidly following injury, accompanied by bacterial accumulation at wound sites and local immune activation. This response resembles a fundamental feature of innate immunity, whereby tissue damage triggers rapid defences against microbial invasion49. However, this microbial interaction entails substantial costs. Whereas moderate guaiacol production enhances immune defence, severe injury elevates guaiacol emission beyond a threshold that attracts conspecifics and promotes cannibalism. Guaiacol thus functions as an intraspecific kairomone-like cue, benefiting receivers at the expense of injured individuals, despite its microbial origin. It is possible that guaiacol also functions as a damage-associated cue that allows injured locusts to anticipate infection and reinforce immune defences, although this remains to be tested. For cannibals, consumption of injured conspecifics may provide both nutritional benefits and beneficial E. hormaechei, potentially enhancing immune competence. Severely injured individuals may also be easier to capture. From the bacterial perspective, guaiacol-mediated attraction could facilitate transmission to new hosts through cannibalistic interactions, suggesting a potential microbial advantage that warrants further investigation.

In a recent development, the phase specificity of guaiacol-mediated attraction may reflect fundamental differences in locust social ecology14. Solitarious locusts generally avoid conspecifics and rarely engage in cannibalism and therefore have limited opportunities to acquire nutrients or beneficial microorganisms through such interactions14. Their comparatively lower immune competence36 may also increase the risks associated with exposure to injured individuals. Consequently, avoidance rather than attraction may be favoured in the solitarious phase.

Our previous work identified PAN as an anticannibalistic pheromone14. As cannibalism and PAN production both increase with swarm density, the opposing effects of PAN and guaiacol suggest a dynamic balance between inhibitory and attractive signals. In insects, attractive and aversive odours are processed through distinct antennal lobe pathways50 and integrated in higher-order centres, including the lateral horn51. We propose that PAN-mediated inhibition normally restrains cannibalism, whereas elevated guaiacol emission following injury may shift this balance towards attraction. How these competing signals are integrated remains an notable question.

Recent findings suggest that we identify LmOR34 and LmOR36 as essential receptors for guaiacol detection, with disruption of either receptor nearly abolishing olfactory attraction and guaiacol-induced cannibalism. Notably, both receptors also detect 2,4,6-TMP, which induces attraction without cannibalism. Similar ligand-dependent behavioural divergence has been reported in D. melanogaster23,24, in which peripheral tuning and central circuit integration contribute to odour discrimination25,26. Guaiacol and 2,4,6-TMP may therefore generate distinct activation patterns or recruit other receptors, enabling ligand-specific behavioural outputs. Moreover, robust guaiacol attraction was restricted to gregarious nymphs, suggesting developmental-, sex- and phase-dependent modulation of olfactory processing. Although antennal lobe odour representations are broadly conserved during locust development27, state-dependent central processing, as demonstrated in D. melanogaster20,52, may contribute to these differences. Developmental expansion of antennal lobe glomeruli may further influence odour coding.

Our findings also help to reconcile previous discrepancies concerning guaiacol emission and behavioural function. Earlier studies reported substantial guaiacol release from intact gregarious locusts and faeces27,53, whereas baseline emissions were considerably lower in our experiments. This difference may reflect sampling conditions: prolonged collective housing in earlier studies could have facilitated biting, injury-associated microbial activation and volatile accumulation20, whereas our shorter collection periods prevented cannibalistic interactions. Thus, elevated guaiacol emission in dense groups may partly reflect socially induced injury rather than constitutive production.

Previous studies also described guaiacol as a behavioural inhibitor10, in contrast to the attraction observed here. However, olfactory responses can vary with physiological and ecological context16,53. We observed significant guaiacol attraction only in starved gregarious nymphs, consistent with the strong association between nutritional stress and locust cannibalism14. State-dependent changes in odour valence have been well documented in insects; for example, starvation reverses the aversive response to acetic acid in D. melanogaster54. Similar physiological modulation of olfactory circuits may explain the context-dependent behavioural effects of guaiacol.

Recent findings suggest that several questions remain unresolved, in particular, how E. hormaechei is recruited from the haemolymph to wound sites and whether guaiacol directly informs injured hosts of tissue damage. Understanding these processes, together with neural integration of guaiacol and anticannibalistic signals, will further clarify how microbial communication coordinates immune and behavioural responses.

Sources indicate that gregarious and solitarious L. migratoria used in this study were originally collected in Guangxi, China, and subsequently maintained at the Shenzhen Agricultural Genomics Institute, Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences. For establishment of stable phase lines, locusts were reared under strictly controlled density conditions for at least three laboratory generations before experimentation. Gregarious locusts were maintained at high population density in ventilated cages (35 cm × 35 cm × 50 cm), each containing 400–500 first-instar nymphs. Solitarious locusts were reared individually in cylindrical containers (10.8-cm height, 8-cm diameter) equipped with independent ventilation to prevent exposure to crowding-associated visual, tactile or olfactory cues. All locusts were kept under standardized environmental conditions, including a 14 h:10 h light/dark photoperiod, temperature of 30 ± 2 °C and relative humidity of 50 ± 5%. Fresh wheat seedlings were provided ad libitum as food throughout rearing and experimental periods. For experiments involving allocation of locusts or biological samples to different treatment groups, individuals or samples were randomly assigned to experimental groups where applicable. Experimental animals were selected from the same phase, developmental stage and rearing conditions, and relevant experimental variables, including feeding status, environmental conditions and experimental procedures, were standardized across treatment groups. For dual-choice behavioural assays, the positions of treatment and control stimuli were alternated between successive trials to minimize positional bias. In experiments in which groups were intrinsically defined by genotype, injury status or severity, microbial status, pathogen treatment, developmental stage, time point, or other experimentally imposed conditions, random allocation to the defining condition was not applicable. In these experiments, comparisons were performed using animals or samples matched for relevant biological characteristics and maintained under otherwise identical experimental conditions. No additional covariate-based allocation was required because the major potential covariates relevant to each experiment were controlled by the experimental design.

Predatory preferences of gregarious L. migratoria nymphs were quantified using dual-choice predation assays conducted in a rectangular acrylic arena (20 cm × 10 cm × 10 cm) under well-ventilated laboratory conditions. Fifth-instar gregarious nymphs were used as predators, whereas gregarious prey nymphs of defined developmental stages (first to fifth instar, depending on the experiment) were used as prey. Before each assay, predator nymphs were starved for 24 h to standardize feeding motivation. To assess predation preference between intact and injured prey, ten fifth-instar gregarious nymphs were introduced into the arena as predators. Two prey nymphs were placed at opposite ends of the arena: one prey individual was left intact, whereas the other was injured. Injuries were generated either mechanically using a sterile scalpel or by controlled conspecific attack, producing wounds of comparable size at a standardized location on the abdominal cuticle. To eliminate potential confounding effects arising from differences in locomotor ability, prey individuals were immobilized at fixed positions using adhesive tape. Predation assays were performed using predators that were either intact or had been subjected to sensory manipulations, including antennal ablation to disrupt primary olfactory input, knockout of olfactory coreceptor LmOrco to impair odorant-receptor-mediated olfaction, or removal of the compound eyes to disrupt visual input. To test whether injury-associated chemical cues influenced predation decisions, dual-choice assays were conducted using guaiacol-treated and solvent-treated prey. In these experiments, 10 predators were simultaneously presented with two prey nymphs, one perfumed with 2 μl of 10−4 guaiacol and the other treated with solvent alone as a control. To evaluate the contribution of gut microbiota to predation preference, we performed further dual-choice assays using germ-depleted prey. For comparisons between E. hormaechei-infected and control prey, ten predators were presented with two injured prey nymphs, one infected with E. hormaechei and the other treated with sterile LB medium. To determine the role of bacterial guaiacol biosynthesis, we further compared predation preference between injured prey infected with wild-type E. hormaechei and a vdc-mutant strain. All microbiota-related assays were conducted as described above, except that prey individuals were allowed to move freely during the assay. In all experiments, prey individuals were weighed immediately before introduction into the arena. After a predation period of 1 h, remaining prey were retrieved and reweighed. Predation preference is expressed as the percentage of total prey body mass consumed for each prey individual. All assays were video-recorded and analysed using EthoVision XT 18.0 software (Noldus Information Technology). Behavioural parameters including attack latency, bite frequency and cumulative bite duration, and the spatial distribution of predator–prey interactions were quantified from the recordings.

Sources indicate that behavioural responses of L. migratoria to volatile compounds were assessed using a two-choice olfactometer14,20. The apparatus consisted of two plastic odour source containers (28 cm × 28 cm × 18 cm) with open tops, each seamlessly connected to a central glass behavioural observation chamber (60 cm × 30 cm × 30 cm). The top of each container was covered with a perforated plastic plate (1-mm-diameter holes spaced 1 cm apart) to allow uniform airflow into the observation chamber. Clean air was supplied to each odour source container from a compressed air cylinder and sequentially filtered through a charcoal filter and a molecular sieve for removal of contaminants. Airflow through each side of the arena was regulated by a flowmeter at a constant rate of 4 l min−1. The glass chamber enclosed the region above the perforated plates and served as the behavioural observation zone. Two fans mounted at the top of the chamber generated a stable vertical airflow, ensuring homogeneous odour distribution. A high-definition digital video camera positioned between the fans continuously recorded locust behaviour. All assays were conducted in a dedicated observation room (60 cm × 70 cm × 80 cm) equipped with a ventilation system and uniform illumination provided by ceiling-mounted white light panels. Before each assay, individual locusts were starved for 24 h. Individual locusts were gently introduced into the centre of the observation chamber and allowed to explore freely for 10 min. During each assay, a control odour (intact fourth-instar prey, paraffin oil or LB medium, depending on the experiment) was delivered to one side of the olfactometer, while the test odour was delivered to the opposite side through the vertical airflow. Test odour sources included volatiles emitted from 6 intact or injured 4th-instar gregarious nymphs, guaiacol applied at concentrations ranging from 10−7 to 10−2 (dilution), or bacterial suspensions (cultured with 15 ppm vanillic acid) at 105 CFU ml−1. Odorants were applied to a piece of filter paper (3 cm × 3 cm) placed inside the corresponding odour source container. To minimize positional bias, we alternated the locations of the odorant and control sides between successive trials. After 8–10 individuals had been tested, the containers were thoroughly cleaned with 75% ethanol and ventilated for 30 min for elimination of residual odours. Locust behaviour was recorded at 30 frames per second, and the total time spent on each side of the arena was quantified manually and used as the behavioural response metric. For group-choice assays, five gregarious nymphs were released simultaneously into the observation chamber. Behavioural recordings were analysed using EthoVision XT 18.0 software (Noldus Information Technology), and the average residence time of the group on each side of the olfactometer was used for quantitative analysis. In the two-choice behavioural assay, locust behaviour was recorded for 10 min (600 s). During this period, most locusts remained either on the odour-treated side or on the control side. Consequently, the sum of the time spent on the odour-treated and control sides was 600 s for most individuals, explaining why the corresponding raw behavioural data frequently summed to 600 s.

Recent findings suggest that to assess whether guaiacol promoted cannibalism under semi-field conditions, predation assays were conducted in outdoor mesh enclosures (1.8 m × 1.2 m × 1.5 m). Each enclosure contained 100 4th-instar gregarious nymphs as prey and 500 5th-instar gregarious nymphs as predators. Before each assay, predator nymphs were starved for 24 h for standardization of feeding motivation. In the control group, all prey nymphs were treated with 2 μl of solvent, whereas in the guaiacol group, each prey nymph was treated with 2 μl of a 10−4 dilution of guaiacol applied to the dorsal thorax. After 24 h, the remaining live 4th-instar nymphs were recovered and counted. The cannibalism ratio was calculated as the proportion of prey nymphs lost after 24 h relative to the initial number released.

According to recent reports, volatile compounds emitted from locust bodies, haemolymph, gut-derived microbial cultures, and bacterial cultures were analysed using SPME coupled with GC–MS. For whole-body volatile analysis, defined numbers of gregarious L. migratoria (1st to 5th instar and adult) or germ-depleted 4th-instar nymphs were placed into 100-ml glass bottles. A 65-µm polydimethylsiloxane/divinylbenzene (PDMS/DVB) SPME fibre (Supelco) was inserted into the bottle headspace through the cap using a PEAK guide piece to prevent direct contact with the insects. Headspace volatiles were collected at 30 °C for 1 h.

In a recent development, for analysis of volatiles derived from gut- and haemolymph-associated microbial communities, gut contents and haemolymph samples were collected aseptically and cultured in LB medium at 30 °C with shaking at 200 rpm for 12 h. The resulting enrichment cultures were transferred to 20-ml headspace vials, and headspace volatiles were collected for 30 min using the same PDMS/DVB SPME fibre. For screening of guaiacol-producing bacterial strains, isolates were cultured in LB medium containing 15 ppm vanillic acid at 30 °C with shaking at 200 rpm for 12 h. A 5-ml aliquot of each bacterial suspension was then transferred to a 20-ml headspace vial, and volatile compounds were collected for 30 min. Volatiles of the control strain lacking vdc were analysed by the same method.

In a recent development, for direct haemolymph volatile analysis, approximately 100 µl of haemolymph was collected from 20 gregarious 4th-instar nymphs and transferred on to a filter paper (2 cm × 5 cm) placed in a 20-ml glass vial. A 65-µm PDMS/DVB SPME fibre was inserted into the vial headspace, and volatile collection was performed at 30 °C for 30 min. For analysis of volatile emissions from E. coli strains expressing the vdc gene cluster, bacterial cultures were grown in LB medium at 37 °C with shaking at 200 rpm until the optical density at 600 nm reached 0.6–1.0. Isopropyl β-d-1-thiogalactopyranoside was then added to a final concentration of 0.5 mM to induce expression of Vdc. After 6 h of induction, vanillic acid was supplemented to a final concentration of 15 mg l−1, and incubation was continued for a further 6 h. A 5-ml aliquot of the induced culture was subsequently transferred to a 20-ml headspace vial, and volatiles were collected for 30 min using the same SPME fibre.

Industry observers note that volatiles from all samples except microorganism-related samples were analysed using a Thermo Scientific Orbitrap GC–MS system equipped with a WAX capillary column (30 m × 0.25-mm inner diameter, 0.25-µm film thickness). The oven temperature program consisted of an initial hold at 50 °C for 3 min, ramping to 150 °C at 5 °C min−1, followed by an increase to 260 °C at 10 °C min−1 and a final hold at 260 °C for 5 min. Volatile compounds were identified by comparison with synthetic standards and by matching of mass spectra to the NIST 2020 mass spectral library. Synthetic reference compounds were obtained from Sigma-Aldrich.

Volatiles from microorganism-related samples, including E. hormaechei, K. pneumoniae and E. coli cultures, were analysed using a SHIMADZU Nexis GC-2030 system equipped with a DB-5 capillary column (30 m × 0.25-mm inner diameter, 0.25-µm film thickness). The oven temperature was held at 40 °C for 3 min, increased to 150 °C at 5 °C min−1 and held for 1 min, then ramped to 260 °C at 10 °C min−1 with a final hold of 5 min. Chemical identification was performed by comparison with synthetic standards and NIST library matches.

To generate germ-depleted fourth-instar L. migratoria nymphs, we applied a cocktail of antibiotics (tetracycline, streptomycin and ciprofloxacin)17,18,19 to autoclaved wheat seedlings, which were then provided as food to second instar nymphs. Antibiotic-treated seedlings were supplied continuously until the insects reached the fourth instar. At this stage, six nymphs were randomly selected for GC–MS analysis to verify depletion of guaiacol-emitting microbiota. Only nymphs in which guaiacol emission was no longer detectable were considered to be germ-depleted and used for downstream experiments.

In a recent development, antennae were dissected from gregarious L. migratoria nymphs (10–20 antennal pairs in total) and pooled for RNA extraction. Total RNA was isolated using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. First-strand cDNA was synthesized from 5 µg of pooled total RNA using a HiScript III 1st Strand cDNA Synthesis Kit (Vazyme Biotech). Gene-specific amplification of odorant receptor (LmOR) coding sequences was performed using 2× Phanta Max Master Mix (Dye Plus) with primers designed on the basis of the antennal transcriptomic dataset. PCR products were separated by 1.0% (w/v) agarose gel electrophoresis, excised and purified before being subcloned into a blunt-end cloning vector (TransGen Biotech). All inserts were confirmed by Sanger sequencing. For each LmOR gene, sequences from at least four independent bacterial clones were aligned to enable us to distinguish genuine sequence polymorphisms from PCR-induced artefacts.

Industry observers note that the entire olfactory receptor coding sequences were cloned into the pUAST.attB expression vector (a gift from J. Bischof) with both XbaI and NotI restriction sites (New England Biolabs). Transgenic D. melanogaster lines harbouring UAS-ORX constructs integrated into chromosome II were generated by the CAS Center for Excellence in Molecular Cell Science (https://sjzx.sibcb.ac.cn/Cn/Index/pageView/catid/105.html). To achieve targeted expression of ORX in at1 olfactory neurons, we crossed each transgenic UAS-ORX line with the Or67d-GAL4 driver line (provided by B. J. Dickson). Through successive genetic screening and selection, we established stable homozygous transgenic lines in which the olfactory receptor transgene was specifically expressed in at1 neurons. The presence and sequence integrity of the transgenes were confirmed by genomic DNA extraction and sequencing of adult flies.

To characterize the functional properties of individual locust olfactory receptors in the Drosophila empty neuron system, we performed SSRs from T1 sensilla of adult flies following established protocols with minor modifications14,20. Briefly, adult flies were immobilized in pipette tips, and the third antennal segment was positioned stably on a glass coverslip. Sensillum subtypes were visualized under an Olympus BX51WI microscope at ×100 magnification and unequivocally identified using diagnostic odorants detailed in Extended Data Table 2. Extracellular recordings of olfactory sensory neuron activity were acquired by insertion of a tungsten microelectrode into the base of the target sensillum, with a reference electrode placed in the compound eye. Signals were amplified (Syntech Universal AC/DC Probe), digitized (96,000 samples per second), and filtered (500–3,000 Hz) using an Intelligent Data Acquisition Controller (Syntech) connected to a computer. Neural spike data were extracted and analysed using AutoSpike software (v.32, Syntech).

Synthetic odorant compounds were freshly diluted in paraffin oil (Sigma-Aldrich). For each stimulation, 10 µl of the diluted odorant was freshly loaded on to a 1-cm2 piece of filter paper and inserted into a glass Pasteur pipette. Odour delivery was achieved by introducing the pipette tip into a constant, humidified airstream (600 ml min−1) flowing through a stainless steel tube with an 8-mm inner diameter, positioned 1 cm from the fly antenna. Neural activity was recorded for 10 s, encompassing a 3-s prestimulation baseline period followed by a 0.5-s odour pulse. Olfactory sensory neuron responses were quantified as the fold change in action potential frequency (spikes per second) relative to the prestimulation baseline. Raw traces were processed by means of amplitude-based spike sorting in AutoSpike, with subsequent data analysis performed in Microsoft Excel and visualization using Adobe Illustrator CS (Adobe Systems).

In addition, SSRs were conducted on basiconic and trichoid sensilla of locusts using functional ligands identified in the Drosophila empty neuron. Locusts were restrained in 1-ml plastic tubes, with their antennae immobilized using dental wax. Recording parameters and data analysis pipelines were identical to those used for Drosophila SSRs.

In a recent development, electroantennograms were recorded from the fifth-instar nymph of the locust. Briefly, the locust antenna was transected at the base of the flagellum, and the freshly cut end was immediately inserted into a glass capillary filled with locust Ringer’s solution (0.1 mol l−1 KCl). Of two such capillaries containing Ag–AgCl electrodes, one served as the ground electrode, and the other was linked to a high-impedance DC amplifier (10× gain; Syntech). Signals were transmitted to an IDAC-4 analog-to-digital converter (Syntech) and subsequently acquired by a computer. Raw data were analysed and archived using EAGPro software (v.3.7, Syntech).

Recent findings suggest that odorant delivery followed a standardized protocol: 10 µl of diluted odorant (prepared as described in the ‘Single-sensillum recordings’ section) was loaded on to a 1-cm2 filter paper, which was inserted into a glass Pasteur pipette, and the pipette tip was introduced into a constant, humidified airstream (600 ml min−1) flowing through a stainless steel tube with an 8-mm inner diameter. The tube outlet was positioned 1 cm from the antenna to ensure consistent stimulus delivery. EAG recordings were 10 s in duration, comprising a 3-s prestimulation baseline and a 0.5-s odour pulse.

Mutant lines of LmOrco, LmOR34, LmOR36 and LmOR39 were generated using CRISPR–Cas9-mediated genome editing with minor modifications to established protocols14,20. Fertilized eggs were collected from freshly deposited egg pods, surface-sterilized with 75% (v/v) ethanol and arranged on 1% (w/v) agarose gels for microinjection. Cas9 protein (150 ng μl−1) and gene-specific single-guide RNAs (400 ng μl−1; target sequences provided in Extended Data Table 3) were coinjected into individual embryos (approximately 27.2 nl per embryo) using a nanolitre microinjector (SYS-PV850, World Precision Instruments) fitted with custom-pulled borosilicate glass capillaries under a stereomicroscope. Injected embryos were incubated at 30 °C until hatching (approximately 12 days).

It has been revealed that G0 nymphs were reared under standardized laboratory conditions in mesh cages (35 cm × 35 cm × 50 cm) under a 14 h:10 h light/dark photoperiod, with ad libitum access to fresh wheat seedlings at 30 °C and 60% relative humidity. Genomic DNA was extracted from adult leg tissue by alkaline lysis (45-μl mixture of 50 mM NaOH and 0.2 mM EDTA, 95 °C for 20 min), followed by neutralization with 5 μl of 1 M Tris-HCl (pH 8.0). A 2-μl aliquot of the resulting lysate was used as a template for PCR amplification of the target genomic loci.

Sources indicate that PCR reactions (25 μl total volume) contained 12.5 μl of 2× Phanta Max Master Mix (Dye Plus), 1 μl each of gene-specific forward and reverse primers (10 μM), and 8.5 μl of nuclease-free water. Thermocycling conditions were as follows: initial denaturation at 95 °C for 3 min; 38 cycles of 95 °C for 15 s, 60 °C for 15 s and 72 °C for 45 s; followed by a final extension at 72 °C for 5 min.

Sources indicate that PCR amplicons were subjected to Sanger sequencing, and mutations were verified by alignment with the wild-type reference sequence. Confirmed G0 mutants were crossed with wild-type individuals to generate G1 progeny, and a distinct deletion allele was used to track inheritance. G1 heterozygotes were intercrossed, and homozygous mutants were identified in the G2 generation by locus-specific PCR genotyping (primer sequences provided in Extended Data Table 3). Stable homozygous mutant lines were established through repeated intercrossing and confirmed by sequencing.

Recent findings suggest that intestinal contents and haemolymph were collected from a population from our laboratory (Shenzhen, Guangdong, China). Another six geographically distinct locust populations from across China were also collected, and the total DNA was extracted from the locust intestinal contents using a QIAamp Fast DNA Stool Mini Kit (Qiagen) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. DNA concentration was measured with a NanoDrop 2000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific), and DNA integrity was assessed by agarose gel electrophoresis. Genomic DNA was fragmented using a Covaris S220 Focused-Ultrasonicator (Covaris) and purified with Agencourt AMPure XP beads (Beckman Coulter). Metagenomic libraries were prepared using a TruSeq Nano DNA LT Sample Preparation Kit (Illumina) following standard protocols. Library construction, high-throughput sequencing and initial data processing were performed by OE Biotech.

Industry observers note that libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform to generate 150-bp paired-end reads. Raw sequencing reads (FASTQ format) were quality-filtered for removal of low-quality bases and adapter sequences using Trimmomatic (v.0.36). Host-derived reads were identified by alignment to the L. migratoria reference genome using Bowtie2 (v.2.2.9) and subsequently discarded. The remaining high-quality, host-depleted reads were assembled de novo into metagenomic scaffolds using MEGAHIT (v.1.1.2). Scaffolds were split at internal gaps into contiguous sequences (scaftigs), and only scaftigs with lengths at least 500 bp were retained for downstream analyses.

In a recent development, open reading frames were predicted from the assembled scaftigs using Prodigal (v.2.6.3) and translated into amino acid sequences. For construction of a non-redundant gene catalogue, all predicted open reading frames were clustered using CD-HIT (v.4.5.7) with a sequence identity threshold of 95% and a coverage cutoff of 90%; the longest sequence within each cluster was selected as the representative gene. Clean reads from each sample were then mapped back to the non-redundant gene set using Bowtie2 (v.2.2.9) with a 95% identity threshold to estimate gene abundance.

Taxonomic annotation of the non-redundant gene set was performed by alignment against the NR protein database. Species abundance profiles were inferred on the basis of gene abundance, and taxonomic abundance statistics were summarized across hierarchical levels, including domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species.

Industry observers note that to identify bacterial strains responsible for guaiacol biosynthesis, we isolated microbial communities from the gut contents and haemolymph of fourth-instar gregarious L. migratoria nymphs. Eluted microbial suspensions were initially cultured in LB medium at 37 °C for 12 h for enrichment of bacterial populations. Cultures were then serially diluted 10-fold to 10−5, which represented the highest dilution that still emitted detectable guaiacol. A 10-µl aliquot of the 10−5 dilution was spread on to LB agar plates and incubated overnight at 37 °C. Individual colonies were randomly selected and screened for guaiacol production. Each isolate was grown in LB medium, and headspace volatiles were collected using a SPME fibre, followed by analysis using GC–MS. Isolates confirmed to emit guaiacol were subjected to whole-genome sequencing, and genomic analysis identified the guaiacol-producing strain as E. hormaechei.

Industry observers note that targeted deletion of the vdc gene cluster in E. hormaechei was achieved using a homologous recombination-based allelic exchange strategy. Briefly, a DNA fragment encompassing the vdc gene and its homology arms about 500 bp upstream and downstream was amplified from wild-type E. hormaechei genomic DNA using specific primers (Extended Data Table 3). The resulting fragment was cloned into the TOPO vector, which subsequently served as a template for amplification of sequences containing an ampicillin resistance cassette and the upstream and downstream homology arms of the vdc genes, using primers TOPO-Vdc-F and TOPO-Vdc-R (Extended Data Table 3). These primers were designed with 15- or 18-nucleotide overhangs at their 5′ ends, homologous to the downstream region and the kanamycin resistance cassette, respectively. The kanamycin resistance cassette from the TOPOloxp-Kana vector was amplified using primers Loxp71F and Loxp66R (Extended Data Table 3). The amplified cassette was then fused with the fragment amplified by TOPO-Vdc-F/R through homologous recombination to generate a circular plasmid.

It has been revealed that the recombinant plasmid was digested with PstI, and the recovered fragment was introduced into E. hormaechei by electroporation (1.8 kV, 25 μF, 200 Ω; Bio-Rad Gene Pulser Xcell or equivalent), and transformants were recovered in antibiotic-free LB medium at 37 °C for 2 h with shaking at 200 rpm. We performed selection for chromosomal integration by plating cells on to LB agar containing 50 mg l−1 kanamycin and incubating them overnight at 37 °C. The single colonies were picked up and cultured in the LB selection broth containing 50 mg l−1 kanamycin and incubated at 37 °C for 12 h. Correct integration events were verified by colony PCR and Sanger sequencing using locus-specific primers Vdc-test.F/R (Extended Data Table 3).

The vdc locus of E. hormaechei comprises three tandemly arranged genes (vdcB, vdcC and vdcD), which together encode the functional decarboxylase complex. To reconstitute this enzymatic system in a heterologous host, we cloned the complete vdc gene cluster and expressed it in E. coli. Primers were designed to amplify the full-length cluster with flanking homology arms compatible with a double-digested pET28a expression vector (Extended Data Table 3), enabling seamless recombination-based insertion of the intact operon. The amplified fragments were purified and assembled into the linearized pET28a backbone by homologous recombination. Recombinant constructs were selected on kanamycin-containing LB agar and sequence-verified by Sanger sequencing to ensure fidelity of the coding regions. Sequence-confirmed plasmids were introduced into E. coli BL21, a strain optimized for inducible protein expression. Transformants were expanded under antibiotic selection, and overnight cultures were used to establish standardized seed cultures for expression assays.

In a recent development, to induce production of the Vdc complex, seed cultures were diluted into fresh LB medium containing kanamycin and grown to mid-log phase (optical density at 600 nm: 0.6–1.0), at which point protein expression was initiated by addition of isopropyl β-d-1-thiogalactopyranoside (final concentration 0.5 mM). Induction was carried out at a reduced temperature (28 °C) to favour proper protein folding and complex assembly. Samples were collected before and after induction to enable direct comparison of expression efficiency. Cells were collected and lysed under conditions designed to preserve protein solubility. Pellets were resuspended in a high-salt glycerol-containing binding buffer supplemented with protease inhibitor and lysozyme, followed by controlled sonication on ice. Soluble and insoluble protein fractions were separated by centrifugation, allowing assessment of Vdc expression levels and solubility. Expression and partitioning of the Vdc proteins were evaluated by SDS–PAGE analysis. Equivalent aliquots of soluble and insoluble fractions were denatured, resolved on precast polyacrylamide gels, and visualized by Coomassie Brilliant Blue staining. Gel images were recorded to document expression of the recombinant Vdc proteins and their distribution between soluble and inclusion body fractions.

Sources indicate that to evaluate the virulence of pathogenic isolates in locusts, fourth-instar nymphs were injected with P. mirabilis (200 nl, 104 CFU ml−1), M. anisopliae (200 nl, 106 CFU ml−1) or E. faecalis (200 nl, 104 CFU ml−1), respectively. Control insects were injected with an equivalent volume of phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). Survival was monitored at 12-h intervals, and each treatment group consisted of 60 or 80 nymphs.

To determine whether guaiacol production by E. hormaechei enhanced host survival following injury, we conducted locust pathogen challenge assays under controlled microbial, dietary, genetic and injury conditions. Germ-depleted nymphs were first generated to eliminate confounding effects of resident microbiota. Wheat seedlings were immersed in either sterile water (control) or sterile water supplemented with wild-type E. hormaechei (103 CFU ml−1), a vdc-mutant strain (103 CFU ml−1) or guaiacol (10−4). After 24 h of feeding on these diets, nymphs were subjected to standardized abdominal wounding, followed by inoculation of the wound site with either P. mirabilis (200 nl, 104 CFU ml−1), M. anisopliae (200 nl, 106 CFU ml−1) or E. faecalis (200 nl, 104 CFU ml−1). Survival was monitored at 12-h intervals, and each treatment group comprised 100–120 nymphs. To directly link mortality outcomes to infection severity, we collected independent cohorts that had been subjected to identical dietary treatments for pathogen load quantification 2 days (P. mirabilis and E. faecalis) or 4 days (M. anisopliae) after inoculation.

Recent findings suggest that to test whether the protective effects of guaiacol and E. hormaechei depended on host innate immune signalling, we performed parallel infection assays in double-stranded RNA (dsRNA)-treated nymphs, targeting components of the Toll and Imd pathways. At 12 h after dsRNA injection, P. mirabilis (100 nl, 104 CFU ml−1) or M. anisopliae (100 nl, 106 CFU ml−1) was delivered using a WPI UMP3 microinjector. Survival was recorded every 12 h, with 80–100 nymphs per treatment, and corresponding cohorts were sampled for haemolymph pathogen load 3 days (P. mirabilis) or 5 days (M. anisopliae) after inoculation.

To further examine whether gregarious predator nymphs benefited from consumption of injured conspecifics that harboured elevated levels of E. hormaechei, germ-depleted fifth-instar predator nymphs were fed equal amounts of either E. hormaechei-colonized prey or germ-depleted prey. Following feeding, predators were challenged by injection with P. mirabilis (300 nl, 104 CFU ml−1) or M. anisopliae (300 nl, 106 CFU ml−1), and survival was monitored at 12-h intervals, with 100–120 individuals per treatment.

Sources indicate that to assess how injury severity modulated immune defence and interacted with microbial protection, we inflicted abdominal wounds of graded size (0.4 mm (level 1) to 1.4 mm (level 6)) before pathogen exposure. P. mirabilis (200 nl, 104 CFU ml−1) or M. anisopliae (200 nl, 106 CFU ml−1) was inoculated directly at the wound site. Ten nymphs were housed per net cage (15 cm diameter, 17 cm height) as one biological replicate, with 6 replicates per treatment. Survival was quantified at 3 days for P. mirabilis and 5 days for M. anisopliae. For determination of the specific contribution of microbial guaiacol production to wound-size-dependent immunity, germ-depleted fourth-instar nymphs were colonized with either wild-type or vdc-mutant E. hormaechei before graded injury and pathogen challenge, with the same experimental design and survival end points.

Pathogen loads in locust haemolymph were quantified by qPCR for assessment of infection intensity under different experimental conditions. Haemolymph (100 μl) was collected from individual locusts, and genomic DNA was extracted using a FastPure Blood/Cell/Tissue/Bacteria DNA Isolation Mini Kit (Vazyme) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. qPCR was performed on a CFX96 Real-Time PCR System (Bio-Rad). Gene-specific primers targeting pathogen and locust reference genes are listed in Extended Data Table 3. Each qPCR reaction was carried out in a total volume of 20 μl, containing 2 μl of DNA template, 10 μl of Taq Pro Universal SYBR qPCR Master Mix (Vazyme, China), 0.8 μl of primer mix (10 μM each) and 7.2 μl of nuclease-free water. No-template controls were included in every run to enable monitoring of potential reagent contamination. Thermal cycling conditions consisted of an initial denaturation followed by 40 amplification cycles of 95 °C for 10 s, 55 °C or 60 °C for 30 s (depending on the primer set) and 72 °C for 20 s. We performed melting curve analysis at the end of each run to confirm amplification specificity. All qPCR assays were conducted with three technical replicates per sample.

In a recent development, absolute quantification of pathogen and host gene copy numbers was performed using standard curves generated from purified plasmid standards. PCR amplicons corresponding to each target gene were amplified with specific primers (Extended Data Table 3) and gel-purified using an EasyPure Quick Gel Extraction Kit (TransGen), cloned into a blunt-end vector and transformed into E. coli DH5α competent cells. Plasmids were extracted using a HiPure Plasmid EF Mini Kit (Magen) and quantified using a NanoDrop 1000 spectrophotometer. Five-fold serial dilutions of each plasmid standard, ranging from 2 ng μl−1 to 6.4 × 10−4 ng μl−1, were prepared and used to construct standard curves for calculation of gene copy numbers.

In a recent development, we tested the antimicrobial activity of guaiacol using an inhibition zone assay to assess whether it directly inhibited pathogen growth. A guaiacol stock solution (5 × 10−2, v/v) was prepared in absolute ethanol, with ethanol alone serving as the vehicle control. LB agar (for bacterial growth) and potato dextrose agar (for fungal growth) were prepared and sterilized by autoclaving. After the molten media had been cooled to approximately 70 °C, 200 μl of either guaiacol stock solution or absolute ethanol was added to 100 ml of molten medium, followed by gentle mixing, and the mixture was poured into plates.

After the agar had solidified, P. mirabilis and M. anisopliae were inoculated individually at the centres of LB and potato dextrose agar plates, respectively. Plates were incubated at 30 °C under constant temperature conditions. Pathogen growth was quantified by measurement of colony diameters at 12 h for P. mirabilis and at 7 days for M. anisopliae; the different measurement times reflected the different growth rates of the bacterial and fungal pathogens.

According to recent reports, to determine whether E. hormaechei responded to host injury, we created artificial wounds on the abdomens of fourth-instar nymphs. Haemolymph was collected from the wound sites 2 h, 4 h, 6 h and 8 h after injury, with samples collected immediately after wounding serving as the 0-h control. For each biological replicate, 100 µl of haemolymph was collected from 20 individual locusts. Three biological replicates were performed. The collected haemolymph was used for DNA extraction and bacterial quantification.

In a recent development, to assess whether E. hormaechei accumulated at wound sites, we again made artificial injuries on the abdomens of fourth-instar nymphs. Haemolymph was collected 6 h after injury from both the wound site and the uninjured pronotum of each locust. A total of 100 µl haemolymph from 20 locusts was pooled to form one biological replicate, and eight replicates were performed. Samples were then processed for DNA extraction and bacterial quantification as described (primer sequences are provided in Extended Data Table 3).

Industry observers note that seven geographically distinct locust populations across China were collected, and the gut contents of the locusts were dissected for DNA extraction. For each biological replicate, 200 mg of gut contents were collected from about 15 individual locusts. Three biological replicates were performed. The collected gut contents were used for DNA extraction and bacterial quantification.

Recent findings suggest that to determine whether guaiacol enhanced resistance to pathogenic microorganisms by activating the locust immune response, we performed transcriptome analyses on wound tissues under different treatment conditions. Germ-free locust nymphs were prepared, and standardized artificial wounds were inflicted on the abdomen. Wound sites were subsequently treated with either PBS (control) or guaiacol (10−4, v/v). Wound tissues were dissected and collected from both PBS- and guaiacol-exposed locusts at 3 h, 6 h and 9 h after treatment. For the subsequent infection assay, P. mirabilis (200 nl, 104 CFU ml−1) was inoculated at the wound site 3 h after initial guaiacol or PBS treatment. Wound tissues were collected from both PBS- and P. mirabilis-exposed locusts at 3 h after treatment.

According to recent reports, total RNA was extracted from wound tissues using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen). RNA quality and concentration were assessed using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer and an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). RNA sequencing libraries were constructed using a NEBNext Ultra RNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina (NEB) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. After quality inspection on an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer, qualified libraries were amplified using phi29 to generate DNA nanoballs, each containing more than 300 copies of a single DNA molecule. DNA nanoballs were loaded on to patterned nanoarrays, and paired-end reads of 100 bp were generated on the DNBSEQ sequencing platform.

In a recent development, raw sequencing reads were processed using SOAPnuke (v.1.4.0) for removal of adapter sequences and low-quality reads. Clean reads were then aligned to the reference genome using HISAT2 (v.2.0.4). Reference genome sequences and gene annotations were obtained from the corresponding genome database. For quantification of gene expression, clean reads were further aligned to the reference coding gene set using Bowtie2 (v.2.2.5), and transcript abundance was estimated using RSEM (v.1.2.12) and normalized as fragments per kilobase of transcript per million mapped reads.

According to recent reports, differential gene expression analysis between guaiacol- and PBS-treated samples was performed using DESeq2 based on a negative binomial generalized linear model. Genes with an adjusted P value (Benjamini–Hochberg correction) less than or equal to 0.05 and an absolute Q value (adjusted P value) less than or equal to 0.05 were considered to be differentially expressed. Functional enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes was conducted using the clusterProfiler R package (v.4.8.1), with correction for gene length bias. Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathways with corrected P < 0.05 were considered to be significantly enriched. KEGG annotations were obtained from the KEGG database for contextualization of transcriptional changes associated with immune and signalling pathways.

It has been revealed that to evaluate the functional contribution of immune-related genes to pathogen resistance, we performed RNAi using gene-specific dsRNA. Total RNA was extracted from locusts using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen), and first-strand cDNA was synthesized from 1 µg of total RNA using a HiScript III 1st Strand cDNA Synthesis Kit (Vazyme). Approximately 500-bp fragments of each target gene were amplified by PCR using gene-specific primers containing T7 promoter sequences (Extended Data Table 3). dsRNA was synthesized using the T7 RiboMAX Express RNAi System (Promega, USA), with dsRNA targeting GFP serving as a negative control.

According to recent reports, dsRNA was injected into fourth-instar nymphs using a WPI UMP3 microinjector. For assessment of knockdown efficiency, abdominal tissues excluding the gut were collected, and transcript levels were quantified by real-time qPCR. Ribosomal protein L32 (RPL32) and β-actin were used as internal reference genes. Each real-time qPCR reaction was performed in a total volume of 20 µl, containing 2 µl of template cDNA, 10 µl of Taq Pro Universal SYBR qPCR Master Mix (Vazyme, China), 0.8 µl of primer mix (10 µM) and 7.2 µl of nuclease-free water. Amplification was carried out for 40 cycles under the following conditions: 95 °C for 10 s, 55 °C or 60 °C for 30 s, and 72 °C for 20 s. Three technical replicates were performed for each sample. No-template controls were included in each run, and melting curve analysis was conducted to confirm amplification specificity. Relative gene expression levels were calculated using the 2−ΔΔCt method.

After confirming effective gene knockdown, we injected dsRNA into a separate cohort of fourth-instar nymphs (n = 80 to n = 100), which were subsequently subjected to pathogen infection assays. Survival rates of dsRNA-treated and control nymphs were recorded to determine the contribution of the targeted genes to resistance against pathogen infection.

Recent findings suggest that to assess whether injury severity affected prey mobility in predation assays, we quantified the locomotor performance of prey nymphs with graded injury levels (levels 1–6). Injured prey nymphs were individually introduced into a well-ventilated arena (56 cm × 28 cm × 18 cm), and their movement trajectories were recorded using a high-definition camera under standardized conditions. Recorded videos were subsequently analysed using EthoVision XT 18.0 software for quantification of total movement distance and average movement speed for each injury level.

All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS 26.0. Statistical analyses were conducted using one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s post hoc test, one-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank test or two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-tests. Preliminary figures were constructed using software Origin 2018 (https://www.originlab.com/), curves were fitted with GraphPad Prism 9.0 and figures were drawn using Adobe Illustrator 2025.

#48754. Process of Elimination

Process of Elimination

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1178 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Arseblog

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, over the course of the November international break, news of contract extensions for some of Arsenal’s ‘pillar’ players has begun to filter through.
  • Arsenal have assembled an elite core and it didn’t happen overnight.
  • Recent findings suggest that in hindsight, it’s interesting that only Ben White and Martin Odegaard have ‘survived’ since then, with Ramsdale, Tomiyasu, Lokonga and Tavares all having drifted away ever since.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, over the course of the November international break, news of contract extensions for some of Arsenal’s ‘pillar’ players has begun to filter through. David Raya, Jurrien Timber, Declan Rice and Piero Hincapie are all reportedly on the verge of new deals, with Riccardo Calafiori’s deal also in the in-tray for Andrea Berta too.

Arsenal have assembled an elite core and it didn’t happen overnight. Back in the summer of 2021, the club enacted a policy of buying players under 24 years old. I always felt like this was the true year zero of the Arteta project. That always felt like the window that built the foundations.

Recent findings suggest that in hindsight, it’s interesting that only Ben White and Martin Odegaard have ‘survived’ since then, with Ramsdale, Tomiyasu, Lokonga and Tavares all having drifted away ever since. Emile Smith Rowe also signed a latest contract and took the number 10 shirt that summer and now he is scratching around for minutes at Fulham.

Recent findings suggest that the summer of 2022 saw the arrivals of Gabriel Jesus and Alex Zinchenko, as well as Fabio Vieira. The former pair briefly elevated Arsenal to a new level before becoming swiftly obsolete. Vieira was a fairly pricey gamble that didn’t pay off. It was the summer of 2023 that truly established Arsenal among England’s elite. David Raya, Jurrien Timber, Declan Rice and Kai Havertz’s arrivals turned Arsenal from caterpillars to butterflies.

Three of those players are about to sign new contracts. Curiously, we have little to no reporting on whether Kai Havertz is lined up for a new deal as yet. Arsenal are banking on their well assembled core to deliver more silverware as they enter their peak years (Raya is 31 which feels close to peak age for a goalkeeper).

Sources indicate that undoubtedly, there are some players who will drift away in the coming years. Mikel Merino, Martin Zubimendi and Ben White feel unlikely to get newly introduced Arsenal contracts at this particular moment in time. (Though these things can and do change). Like Havertz, Odegaard’s deal runs until the summer of 2028 and we have yet to hear rumblings of a new deal.

Industry observers note that odegaard and Havertz have negotiated significant fitness challenges over the last two seasons, which probably explains why they have found themselves lower down Berta’s to do list. Timber has had his own physical challenges too, but he is 25. Havertz and Odegaard are 27. Their next contracts will be their last ‘big’ contracts in terms of wages and their resale value will drop to close to zero if Arsenal tie them down. It makes sense for the club to take its time a little more with both players.

Sources indicate that both are also defining attacking and / or creative players in the Arsenal team. At some point, Arteta is going to have to plot an evolution within this core and it feels like that is more likely to happen in the final third of the pitch than within the core of players who operate behind the ball. Behind the ball, Arsenal are absolutely tip top and have some of the most elite players in the world in their positions.

Recent findings suggest that that is not as true ahead of the ball. Odegaard and Havertz remain, for my money, elite, defining players for Arsenal. For the purposes of this piece; I am going to speculate that Odegaard is going to be offered a fresh contract given his status in the team and because his role is a little more holistic and he doesn’t solely operate in the final third.

Recent findings suggest that which leaves us with Havertz. I rate Havertz really highly and believe he is integral to Arsenal’s style, he has the technical quality to play one touch football and the physical quality to act as a release valve and hold the ball up. I can’t think of many forwards who offer both sides of the game to such an extent.

There are several Arsenal attackers I would trade in before Havertz. However, the market doesn’t always bend to your will. Arsenal remain a self sustaining club and in the PSR / SCR era, player trading has never been more important or more voluminous. Keeping money swishing between the cost and revenue columns is a necessity in this environment.

Sources indicate that clearly, the number one impediment to Havertz getting a upcoming deal is his fitness. He is still clearly preferred by the manager to Viktor Gyokeres. I have to say I am surprised (a little unpleasantly) at how rapidly the tide of opinion has turned against Havertz. The run he went on very recently that saw him score in the Champions League Final, score the goal that clinched the title against Burnley, a critical goal against Chelsea and the winning goal at Anfield seem to have just bought him absolutely no credit within the fan base, which I find a little surprising.

However, Arsenal need to boost their attacking prowess overall at some point very soon. Like I stated, I would consider Havertz a superior player to all of Eze, Gyokeres, Tzolis and Madueke. The squad is well served for numbers in attack; it doesn’t have any gaps in that respect. It has a gap in elite quality.

The key to boosting that might not be ‘who is the least effective player?’ it might be ‘who is the most saleable?’ Sometimes you do just have to cash in your chips on a player to evolve and move forwards. It doesn’t always have to be because the player is obsolete or not good enough. Arsenal have such numbers in midfield that there also isn’t really a route into the team there for Havertz either.

If someone offered £60-70m for Gyokeres or Eze, I would accept it and give Havertz a fresh contract the next day (assuming he does prove his fitness). But I think those scenarios are unlikely. I am not arguing that we have definitely reached the ‘we must sell Kai’ stage and I will reiterate that, at this moment in time, I consider him a very key player who should pretty much always start when fit.

While he isn’t the most prolific finisher as a centre-forward, crucial goals this season against Chelsea and Liverpool demonstrate his worth. The conversation about moving on only becomes live on condition that the money is used to immediately buy an obviously elite attacker- preferably a centre-forward in that case since that is the gap a Havertz departure would leave.

According to recent reports, but I am certain it is a conversation Arteta and Andrea Berta are currently entertaining. Arteta will want to push the level of the team even further and, to fund what that is going to entail, potentially painful sales will have to be made somewhere. The vigour with which the club pursued the sale of Gabriel Martinelli this summer shows the manager has the stomach for that conversation too.

Telstar vs PEC Zwolle - prediction, team news, lineups

  • Matchday 13 of the 2026-27 Eredivisie season sees Telstar host PEC Zwolle at BUKO Stadion on Saturday evening.
  • Both teams begin this weekend’s clash within three points of the automatic relegation places, and neither will want to leave empty-handed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Adepoju Marvellous | 19 Nov 2026 19:38, Last updated: 19 Nov 2026 19:40.

Matchday 13 of the 2026-27 Eredivisie season sees Telstar host PEC Zwolle at BUKO Stadion on Saturday evening.

Both teams begin this weekend’s clash within three points of the automatic relegation places, and neither will want to leave empty-handed.

According to recent reports, A 10-match winless run between August 8 and October 23 dampened any optimism that may have been brewing after Telstar’s season-opening win over NEC. However, they have since responded with four points from a possible six, most recently earning a 2-2 draw against Fortuna Sittard.

Having been tipped by many as the next managerial casualty of 2026-27, Henk Brugge appears to have bought himself some breathing room, but he will know his position remains precarious, and any underwhelming result could still spell the end for him.

Averaging two goals per home league match this term, De Witte Leeuwen have found little difficulty scoring in front of their fans, although much of that good work is being undone by a porous defence that has conceded 17 times across six home games.

Sources indicate that january’s 4-1 defeat marked Telstar’s seventh straight loss against Zwolle and extended their winless run in this fixture to 16 matches across all competitions dating back to February 2007. This weekend’s hosts will need to buck an unpleasant trend to secure all three points.

A 4-2 triumph over FC Utrecht in their most recent home match ended a run of six games without a win for Telstar, who now seek back-to-back victories in Velsen for the first time since beating Sparta Rotterdam and Heracles by a combined score of 7-1 to close out 2025-26 on a high.

It has been revealed that after weeks of searching, PEC Zwolle will have a latest face in the dugout for their upcoming clash against Telstar, with Alex Pastoor recently appointed as head coach until the end of the 2026-27 season. He replaces Henry van der Vegt, whose 15-month tenure ended in October.

Pastoor’s immediate task will be to build on his side’s four-game league unbeaten run, during which they have collected eight points from a possible 12, with only Heerenveen (12) and Ajax (10) boasting a better record in the division.

With three of their next four matches coming against teams currently in the top seven - AZ Alkmaar, Fortuna Sittard, and PSV Eindhoven - De Blauwvingers could use a win here as they look to put some distance between themselves and the drop zone before the end of 2026.

Industry observers note that both of Saturday’s opponents have managed just three clean sheets between them from 24 matches this season, so this weekend’s clash is likely to be decided at the attacking end. On that front, Zwolle have struggled compared to their hosts, scoring five fewer goals so far.

However, the visitors could tilt things in their favour with a quick start, and having scored the opener in four of the last five gameweeks, they may look to capitalise on a Telstar side that has conceded first four times during that span.

Telstar form (all competitions):.

PEC Zwolle form (all competitions):.

Gerald Alders, 21, has missed Telstar’s last four matches and will remain sidelined for Saturday’s clash as he continues his recovery to full fitness.

Rui Mendes is also unlikely to feature for the hosts, though his comeback is not far off after missing the last three matches.

Tyrone Owusu has four goals and one assist in his last six outings, already making this his most productive season in a Telstar shirt.

Deadline-day loan signing Filip Krastev has yet to feature this term due to an Achilles tendon injury sustained while playing for Goztepe.

Givaro Rahajaan and Sherel Floranus are also unavailable this weekend, but both are nearing their respective returns.

Telstar possible starting lineup:.

Koeman Jr; Peersman, Soualhia, Valk, Caschili; Ahmed, Rossen; Martha, Owusu, Brouwer; Thorisson.

PEC Zwolle possible starting lineup:.

Schendelaar; Van der Haar, Viergever, Velthuis, Aertssen; Sommer, Thomas; Mbayo, Namli, Van der Wal; Van Hooijdonk.

Both teams have performed well of late, and neither enters Saturday’s game with their confidence depleted.

With little to separate the sides, a draw appears the most likely outcome, so we are backing a share of the spoils.
